themes.label: Default stance and who decides
themes.desc: Whether AI is allowed by default, who sets the rule (department, instructor, assignment), and whether uses are sorted into levels or categories.

themes.label: Communicating expectations
themes.desc: How and where the rules are made explicit to students.

themes.label: What students may use AI for
themes.desc: Uses that are allowed or encouraged: explanation, debugging help, brainstorming, writing support, course-provided tools.

themes.label: What students may not use AI for
themes.desc: Uses that are ruled out, especially generating code or solutions that are submitted as one's own.

themes.label: Disclosure and attribution
themes.desc: Whether and how AI use must be acknowledged, cited, or documented (prompts, transcripts, reflections).

themes.label: Student accountability and understanding
themes.desc: Students remain responsible for what they submit and must be able to explain and defend it.

themes.label: Assessment design
themes.desc: How assignments, exams, weighting, and formats change in response to AI.

themes.label: Detection and enforcement
themes.desc: Detectors, evidence, academic-integrity processes, sanctions, and amnesty.

themes.label: Why: learning and careers
themes.desc: The reasons given: protecting skill-building and productive struggle, and preparing students for AI-rich professional work.

themes.label: Faculty and staff use of AI
themes.desc: AI use by instructors and TAs for grading, feedback, materials, and course operations.

themes.label: Equity, privacy, ethics, and IP
themes.desc: Access and cost, data and privacy, bias and environmental concerns, and intellectual property.

themes.label: Governance and change over time
themes.desc: Acknowledging that policy will change, review cycles, and who maintains the policy.

phases.label: Before the course
phases.desc: Decisions instructors and departments make while designing the course and its policy.

phases.label: At the start of the course
phases.desc: Communicating expectations to students up front.

phases.label: While students work
phases.desc: Rules that apply while doing assignments, labs, and projects.

phases.label: During assessment
phases.desc: Exams, quizzes, interviews, and other evaluations of individual understanding.

phases.label: When something goes wrong
phases.desc: Suspected misuse, detection, evidence, consequences, and amnesty.

phases.label: Over time
phases.desc: Reflection, review, and revision of the policy as tools and practice change.

actors.label: Addressed to students
actors.desc: Rules and expectations students must follow.

actors.label: Addressed to instructors
actors.desc: Guidance and obligations for faculty designing and running courses.

actors.label: Addressed to TAs and staff
actors.desc: Guidance for teaching assistants, graders, and support staff.

actors.label: Department commitments
actors.desc: What the unit itself commits to or decides.

codebook.label: Default stance
codebook.definition: Whether AI use is allowed or prohibited when nothing else is specified.

codebook.label: Instructor discretion
codebook.definition: The instructor (or assignment) sets the rule; the unit defers to course-level decisions.

codebook.label: Use categories / levels
codebook.definition: Explicit tiers or categories of permitted use (e.g. no AI, limited AI, open AI).

codebook.label: Syllabus communication
codebook.definition: Requirements to state AI expectations in the syllabus or at the start of an assignment.

codebook.label: Permitted uses
codebook.definition: Specific uses of AI that are allowed or encouraged.

codebook.label: Writing assistance
codebook.definition: AI for prose: reports, documentation, editing, grammar.

codebook.label: Course-provided tools
codebook.definition: AI tools supplied or sanctioned by the course or institution (e.g. a course tutor bot).

codebook.label: Prohibited uses
codebook.definition: Specific uses of AI that are not allowed.

codebook.label: Code generation
codebook.definition: Provisions specifically about AI-generated code (Copilot, ChatGPT code).

codebook.label: Disclosure and citation
codebook.definition: Requirements to acknowledge, cite, or document AI use.

codebook.label: Accountability and understanding
codebook.definition: Students are responsible for submitted work and must understand and be able to explain it.

codebook.label: Assessment design
codebook.definition: Changes to assignments, grading weight, or evaluation formats in response to AI.

codebook.label: In-person / proctored exams
codebook.definition: Use of supervised, oral, or in-person evaluation to assess individual understanding.

codebook.label: Detection tools
codebook.definition: Statements about AI detectors, their reliability, or their use.

codebook.label: Integrity and sanctions
codebook.definition: Treatment of misuse as an academic-integrity violation; consequences; amnesty or regret clauses.

codebook.label: Learning rationale
codebook.definition: Reasons grounded in learning: skill-building, practice, productive struggle.

codebook.label: AI literacy and careers
codebook.definition: Preparing students to use AI well, critically, or professionally.

codebook.label: Collaboration analogy
codebook.definition: Treating AI like a person, collaborator, tutor, or other source under existing collaboration rules.

codebook.label: Instructor / staff use
codebook.definition: General statements about AI use by faculty, TAs, or staff.

codebook.label: Faculty grading and feedback
codebook.definition: AI in grading, feedback, or evaluation of student work by instructors or TAs.

codebook.label: Faculty course materials
codebook.definition: AI in creating course content, assignments, or examples.

codebook.label: Equity and access
codebook.definition: Unequal access, paid tools, accessibility, fairness across students.

codebook.label: Privacy and data
codebook.definition: Uploading student work or course materials, FERPA, data retention, approved tools.

codebook.label: Ethics, bias, environment
codebook.definition: Bias, hallucination, harms, environmental and labor concerns.

codebook.label: Intellectual property
codebook.definition: Licensing, ownership, and copyright of AI-generated output or course materials.

codebook.label: Policy evolution
codebook.definition: Policy may change; review cycles; ongoing deliberation.

codebook.label: Research use
codebook.definition: AI in theses, research projects, or graduate work.

patterns.title: Exams stay AI-free, even where homework is open
patterns.body: The most uniform rule in the corpus. Courses that welcome AI on projects still close it off on exams, quizzes, and in-class work. Many are moving more of the grade onto those unassisted settings.

patterns.title: Students own what they submit and must be able to explain it
patterns.body: Whatever the default stance, policies converge on accountability. The student is responsible for correctness and must be able to explain or defend every line, sometimes in a live interview.

patterns.title: Learning, not productivity, is the stated reason for limits
patterns.body: Restrictions are justified almost entirely in terms of skill-building. AI is described as skipping the practice that produces learning, as especially harmful to novices, and as hiding gaps that show up later on exams.

patterns.title: Misuse is handled through existing academic-integrity processes
patterns.body: Few policies invent new enforcement. Unauthorized AI use is treated as plagiarism or unauthorized collaboration, reported through the usual channels, and penalized with familiar sanctions.

patterns.title: Where AI is allowed, disclosure is the price of use
patterns.body: Permissive policies almost always attach a disclosure duty. Its form varies: a statement, a citation with the prompt, the full transcript, or a comment at the exact lines.

patterns.title: AI as a tutor is the most widely permitted use
patterns.body: Even restrictive courses typically allow AI for explaining concepts, error messages, and course material. The usual line falls between asking questions and getting answers.

patterns.title: Universities delegate; computing units decide
patterns.body: University-wide policies mostly hand the decision to instructors: about half defer explicitly to the instructor and about a quarter offer a menu of use levels. Their concrete rules concern syllabus statements, data privacy, and doubts about detectors. Computing departments and courses make the substantive calls themselves: whether code may be generated, whether AI is allowed on exams, and whether students must explain every line. A university policy alone rarely tells a computing student what is allowed.

patterns.title: Default stance: prohibit or embrace?
patterns.body: Courses at the same level, sometimes in the same department, take opposite defaults. Some rule AI out entirely for graded work; others build the course around AI coding agents.

patterns.title: Does disclosure make use acceptable?
patterns.body: Some policies promise that honest disclosure carries no penalty, so nondisclosure becomes the offense. Others hold that disclosed use is still a violation or still earns no credit.

sides.label: Disclosed use can still be penalized

patterns.title: Detecting AI: disavow detectors or deploy them?
patterns.body: Some institutions state that AI detectors are unreliable and promise not to use them. Others say they run tools that look specifically for AI-generated code or text.

patterns.title: Career readiness versus foundational skill
patterns.body: The same appeal to future employment is used on both sides. Some argue graduates must be fluent with AI; others argue employers will keep testing unassisted ability, so the fundamentals must come first.

patterns.title: Treat AI like a person, or write AI-specific rules?
patterns.body: One family of policies maps AI onto existing collaboration rules: if you couldn't ask a friend, don't ask the model. Another writes rules only AI needs, such as word caps on prompts, line limits, percentage caps, and bans on tools reading the codebase.

patterns.title: Monitoring the process versus protecting student data
patterns.body: To verify authorship, some courses log prompts, sessions, or commit histories. Others warn students that AI services store and profile what they are given. Process evidence and privacy pull in opposite directions.

patterns.title: Should instructors grade with AI?
patterns.body: Policies that address faculty use disagree. Some commit that AI will never grade; one discloses AI-assisted grading and offers an opt-out.

patterns.title: Who sets the rule: the instructor or the department?
patterns.body: Many units defer entirely to each instructor. A few impose a shared tier system or department-wide rule, trading local flexibility for consistency students can rely on.

patterns.title: AI for prose: never, or freely?
patterns.body: Writing gets its own rules, but in opposite directions. Some computing courses allow only spelling and grammar checkers; some information-school courses let students generate or rephrase text.

patterns.title: Faculty and TA use of AI is rarely addressed
patterns.body: Nearly every document regulates students. Only a handful say anything about how instructors may use AI for grading, feedback, or course materials, or commit to disclosing it.

patterns.title: Equity, cost, and accessibility are seldom mentioned
patterns.body: Few policies consider students who cannot pay for premium tools, who prefer a human, or who rely on assistive technology with built-in AI.

patterns.title: Amnesty and self-reporting are rare
patterns.body: Almost all enforcement language is punitive. Only a few courses offer a window to come forward or withdraw a submission.

patterns.title: Agentic tools are only starting to appear
patterns.body: Most policies still picture a chatbot. A few address IDE-embedded assistants and autonomous agents that read and edit a whole codebase, a fast-moving area where most policies are silent.

patterns.title: Little evidence, little revision
patterns.body: Policies make strong claims about learning, but few cite their own course data or commit to reviewing the policy on a schedule.

patterns.title: Ethical, environmental, and IP concerns are peripheral
patterns.body: Bias, labor, energy use, and licensing appear in only a few documents, and rarely as rules.

p: This atlas gathers the generative-AI policies that computing departments and courses at universities in the United States and Canada have published, and reconciles them into a shared set of guidelines. The approach follows Amershi et al.'s 'Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction' (CHI 2019): collect many sources, keep their statements verbatim, cluster statements that make the same point, name each cluster, and offer several ways of organizing the result.
It is meant for institutions writing or revising their own AI policy. Each guideline shows how many institutions say something similar, and in what words.

Universities in the United States and Canada. Each university’s documents come from the highest of these source tiers that exists. Tiers 1 and 2 are both computing units, so a university with a CS policy and, say, an iSchool policy keeps both. Tiers 3 and 4 are used only when a university has no computing-unit policy at all.
list: Tier 1: a computer science department policy or CS course policies (including CSE, EECS, and computing colleges).
Tier 2: if there is no CS policy, a CS-related unit such as information science or an iSchool, informatics, AI, data science, or software engineering.
Tier 3: otherwise, a school or college policy that covers computing, such as a College of Engineering policy.
Tier 4: otherwise, the university-wide AI policy.
after: Course policies are capped at three per unit, favoring introductory courses. One exception to the tier rule is kept on purpose: Harvey Mudd College's AI Use Levels pilot, a college-wide document that Pomona College's CS tier system is modeled on. News coverage and research papers are excluded. Every institution checked is listed on the Corpus tab, including those where nothing qualifying was found.

list: Search: parallel research agents searched by region and institution type (northeast, west, midwest, south, Canada, liberal-arts colleges, an open sweep, and computing-adjacent units). A second pass re-searched institutions the first pass could only browse and added new ones. A third pass checked every remaining Carnegie R1 and R2 university in the United States and every Canadian university with a computing degree, and added university-wide policies where no computing policy exists.

Fetch: each included document was fetched as plain text (HTML, PDF, Word, or Google Docs export). JavaScript-only pages were checked in a real browser, and pages that no longer resolve were checked against an Internet Archive snapshot.
Excerpt: from each document, up to eight statements that set policy were excerpted as contiguous quotes of at most fifteen words.

Verify: every excerpt was re-located in an independently re-fetched copy of the page. The page's exact characters replaced the excerpt, and a link was built that opens the original page with the full passage highlighted.
Code: each statement was coded with one to three topics, one course-lifecycle phase, and one addressee (student, instructor, TA or staff, department).

p: Each statement was assigned to exactly one guideline. A first assignment used an explicit rule over each statement's primary code and wording. The analyst then reviewed every cluster and moved misassigned statements; each move is recorded as an override, and the Statement explorer's Guideline view shows the final assignment.

Guideline labels are analyst-written names for clusters, phrased as recommendations. They are not policy text. The evidence for each guideline is always the institutions' own words, and the highlighted quote is the statement judged most representative.

Guidelines are grouped four ways: by theme, by the course-lifecycle phase they apply to (modeled on Amershi et al.'s 'initially / during interaction / when wrong / over time'), by whom they address, and by how widely they are shared. Readers can build and save their own groupings.

Coverage is a snapshot: course policies change every term, and many syllabi sit behind learning-management-system logins, so public documents over-represent courses with public websites. Excerpts are short by design and do not carry the full context of the surrounding policy; follow the source link before citing any statement. Codes and clusters reflect one analyst's reading and should be validated by a second coder before publication.
